Waters of Marah
MAH-ruh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Marah, "bitter"; the place in the wilderness where Israel found bitter water that the LORD made sweet by a tree.

📖 Biblical Definition

Marah was the first stopping-place in the wilderness after Israel crossed the Red Sea, where they found water but could not drink it, "for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah" (Exo 15:23). Three days into the desert with no water, the people murmured against Moses; and Moses cried unto the LORD, "and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet" (Exo 15:25). There God made for them a statute and an ordinance, and proved them, revealing Himself by a new name: "I am the LORD that healeth thee" (Exo 15:26). Marah is one of the richest types in the Old Testament. The bitter waters of a fallen, wilderness world are made sweet only by a tree cast into them — a foreshadowing of the cross of Christ, by which the bitterness of sin, sorrow, and death is transformed into sweetness for the people of God. Marah stands in the dictionary as the place of bitterness made sweet, where God taught Israel that He is the Healer, and where the tree thrown into the bitter waters points to the cross that turns the bitterest providence into a fountain of sweetness for those who trust the LORD.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The wilderness place (Exo 15:23-26) where Israel's bitter water was made sweet by a tree the LORD showed Moses; where God revealed Himself as "the LORD that healeth thee," a type of the cross that turns bitterness to sweetness.

WATERS OF MARAH, proper noun. "Bitter"; the first wilderness camp after the Red Sea (Exo 15:23).

Where Israel found water too bitter to drink and murmured.

Where the LORD showed Moses a tree that made the waters sweet (Exo 15:25).

Where God made a statute and proved His people.

Where God revealed Himself: "I am the LORD that healeth thee" (Exo 15:26).

📖 Key Scripture

Exo 15:23 — "And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah."

Exo 15:25 — "And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet: there he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them,"

Exo 15:26 — "...for I am the LORD that healeth thee."

Gal 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Marah needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God turns the bitter providences of the wilderness to sweetness by the tree of the cross, and reveals Himself as the Healer of His people.

expand to see more

Bitterness-without-hope correction. The natural heart, meeting the bitter waters of affliction, murmurs as Israel did and concludes that God has forgotten. Marah teaches otherwise: the same God who led them to the bitter water provided the tree that made it sweet. The dictionary holds that no bitterness in the believer's path is beyond the sweetening power of God; He who showed Moses the tree still casts the cross of Christ into our bitterest providences, and turns the waters sweet.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the typology of the tree. The tree cast into the bitter waters foreshadows the cross, on which Christ was made a curse for us (Gal 3:13), and by which the curse itself is turned to blessing. The dictionary commends the lesson: at Marah God revealed Himself as the Healer, and the wood that healed the waters points to the wood of Calvary, where the bitterness of sin and death is swallowed up in the sweetness of redeeming grace.
